h1:
Eating Around Phra Pathommachedi
Noodles, Rice & Curry, Night Market
intro: Phra Pathommachedi draws both locals and visitors all year round to pay their respects, but plenty of people come back just as much for the ring of food stalls around the chedi that runs from morning until late. Mornings bring old-school noodle shops and hot rice-and-curry; afternoons it's wonton noodles and sweets; and once evening falls, the night market opens in a long row that's easy to graze your way through. We walked the full loop around the chedi and picked out which shops are the real deal, when to eat them, and what they cost.

blocks.html: The nice thing about eating around the chedi is that everything is within walking distance. The roundabout circling Phra Pathommachedi has four sides, each with a different style of food — one side is old shops that open early, another is the night market that opens in the evening. Time it well and you can park once and eat your way from breakfast to dinner. This guide is split by time of day, so whenever you arrive, just jump to that section.

blocks.text: Morning — Old-School Noodles and Rice & Curry

blocks.html: Nakhon Pathom is genuine noodle country. Many of the famous shops open early and sell out before afternoon, so if you've got your heart set on a particular bowl, come before noon. The rice-and-curry stalls around the chedi are the classic local breakfast too, and prices are still very easy on the wallet.

items.name: Pa Lai Chicken Noodles
items.blurb: Clear, punchy tom yum chicken noodles — a longtime favorite of Nakhon Pathom locals, with people queuing from the morning. The broth is well balanced, the chicken tender, and it's great with crispy wontons on the side.

items.name: Nai Lue Boat Noodles
items.blurb: Traditional boat noodles with a rich, dark broth. The bowls are small and cheap, so it's easy to order several at once — perfect if you like the bold, classic boat-noodle flavor.

items.name: Ko Yao Red Pork Rice
items.blurb: An old-school red pork and crispy pork rice shop right by the chedi. The sauce leans sweet and mellow in the Nakhon Pathom style, and it opens early enough to be your first meal of the day.

items.name: Pa Mali Rice & Curry (chedi, Phra Ruang gate side)
items.blurb: A rice-and-curry pushcart parked in front of the chedi by the Phra Ruang gate, with a wide spread of dishes ladled over hot rice. It's a regular breakfast stop for people coming to make merit at the chedi.
items.meta: In front of the chedi, Phra Ruang gate side · mornings

items.name: Mae Boontham Buffet Rice & Curry
items.blurb: A legendary rice-and-curry buffet in front of Odeon Market beside the chedi — load up on several dishes for one set price. Locals have been eating here for years.
items.meta: In front of Odeon Market · Mon–Fri, morning–afternoon

items.name: Phaya Kong Kuay Chap
items.blurb: A legendary thick-broth kuay chap (rolled rice-noodle soup with offal) in the chedi area, open for over 40 years. Soft noodles, a fragrant peppery broth, and a very low starting price.

blocks.title: Morning tip
blocks.html: Many of the famous noodle shops sell out before afternoon, so if there's one you've specifically got your eye on, come before noon — and bring cash, since most of these old shops still deal mainly in cash.

blocks.text: Midday to Afternoon — Wonton Noodles, Rad Na, Cooling Sweets

blocks.html: Late morning into the afternoon is the time for wonton noodles and rad na. These shops are scattered around the roundabout and in the small sois. Once you've finished paying your respects and the sun starts to bite, you can duck into a market corner for something cold and sweet.

items.name: Jon Yao Wonton Noodles
items.blurb: An old-school wonton noodle shop near the chedi that makes its own noodles and wontons. The noodles are springy, the red pork just sweet enough — it's the name Nakhon Pathom locals think of when wonton noodles come up.

items.name: Bu Rad Na
items.blurb: Wide rice noodles, crisp on the outside and soft inside, with a thick gravy. It's in the night market area, open afternoon into evening, just a few dozen baht a plate.

items.name: Liang Jui (herbal drinks)
items.blurb: Chilled jap liang and herbal drinks to cool off after walking around the chedi — just over ten baht a glass, and a fixture of the market for years.

items.name: Old-Style Toast, Tee Café
items.blurb: Old-style toast with kaya custard and other fillings, starting at just a few baht — a good spot to sip a coffee and rest your feet in the afternoon (closed Wednesdays).

blocks.text: Dinner — The Phra Pathommachedi Night Market

blocks.html: As the sun dips, the night market around the chedi gradually opens — most stalls around 16:30–17:00, running until nine or ten. This is the highlight of eating around the chedi: savory dishes, fried snacks, seafood, and sweets lined up in a row, easy to graze one thing at a time.

items.name: Cho Tod Man Kung (shrimp cakes)
items.blurb: Dense, hot-off-the-fryer shrimp cakes — one of the longest queues in the market. Pick a small or large box and eat them with the sweet-and-sour ajad dip.

items.name: Cho Hoi Tod / Or Suan
items.blurb: Crispy oyster omelette and or suan with fragrant egg and plump oysters — a popular plate many people order first thing in the evening.

items.name: Nai Kim Oyster Omelette
items.blurb: An old-school oyster omelette shop open for over 35 years, with crispy batter and fluffy egg. It's the name people mention when they think of oyster omelette by the chedi — come in the evening and the queue starts to build.
items.meta: Inside the night market · Mon–Fri 17:00–21:30, Sat–Sun 16:30–21:30

items.name: Nai Klae Seafood
items.blurb: Fresh seafood, grilled and stir-fried, at friendly prices — a good spot to sit down for a proper meal with friends or family in the market atmosphere.

items.name: Chen Nguan Flying Ice Cream
items.blurb: The legendary trick-tossing ice cream of the chedi — an old vendor who flips the ice cream through the air as a little show. Kids love it, and it's the dessert that's become this market's signature image.

items.name: Rakhang Thong Mango (mango with sweet fish sauce)
items.blurb: A well-known mango with sweet fish sauce — thick, sticky nam pla wan topped with fragrant dried shrimp, balanced sour-sweet-salty. Buy it to take home or snack on in the market.

items.name: Bai Yok Bua Loy with Sweet Egg
items.blurb: Bua loy in ginger broth and coconut milk with soft sweet egg — a warm dessert to round off dinner, starting at just over ten baht.

items.name: Mae Yupha Thai Sweets
items.blurb: A wide range of old-style Thai sweets, both to take home and to snack on. They're colorful and pretty — easy to grab as a little gift to bring back.

blocks.title: Night market tip
blocks.html: The night market opens daily from around 16:30. Weekends get crowded and some stalls open earlier. If you'd rather not jostle, come in the early evening, 17:00–18:00 — everything's still there and the queues aren't long yet. Parking around the chedi fills up fast in the evening, so leave a little extra time to find a spot.

blocks.text: Eating Around the Chedi All Day — Time It Like This

blocks.html: If you've got a full day, here's a flow that works without moving the car much. Start the morning with something hot, take a midday break, pay your respects in the afternoon, then close out with the night market in the evening.

items.activity: Start with Nai Lue boat noodles or Pa Lai chicken noodles
items.note: Beat the crowd while the broth is still rich

items.activity: Follow up with Ko Yao red pork rice, or stop at Pa Mali rice & curry in front of the chedi
items.note: Keep it light to save room for the next meal

items.activity: Sip a Liang Jui herbal drink to settle the stomach
items.note: Cool off before the sun gets strong

items.activity: Jon Yao wonton noodles or Bu rad na for lunch
Head up to pay respects at Phra Pathommachedi and walk the temple grounds
items.note: The afternoon is shadier than midday

items.activity: Snack break — old-style toast at Tee Café + iced coffee
Enter the night market as it opens, starting with oyster omelette / shrimp cakes
items.note: Queues are still short in the early evening

items.activity: Settle in for Nai Klae seafood as the main meal
items.note: Sit a while with friends or family

items.activity: Finish with dessert — flying ice cream + bua loy with sweet egg
items.note: Grab mango with sweet fish sauce / Thai sweets to take home

blocks.text: What to Know Before You Go Eating

items: Bring cash — most old shops and market stalls still deal mainly in cash. There are ATMs around the chedi just in case.
Timing — morning to afternoon is for the early-opening shops; the night market starts around 16:30. If you want to eat across the whole day, pace your stomach well.
Parking — there's parking around the chedi roundabout, but it fills up fast in the evening. Leave extra time, or park in an outer soi and walk in.
Closing days — some shops close on a midweek day (e.g. the old-style toast spot closes Wednesdays), so check first if there's one you specifically want to hit.

faq.q: What time does the Phra Pathommachedi night market open?
faq.a: Most stalls start opening around 16:30–17:00 and run until about 22:00, every day. Weekends get crowded and some stalls open a little earlier. Come in the early evening for the best selection before the queues build up.

faq.q: When should I come for the old-school noodle shops?
faq.a: Morning to noon is best. Many of the famous noodle shops open early and sell out before afternoon — Pa Lai chicken noodles and Nai Lue boat noodles, for example. Come in the afternoon and you may miss a few of them.

faq.q: Is there morning rice and curry around the chedi?
faq.a: Yes — both Pa Mali rice & curry, parked in front of the chedi by the Phra Ruang gate, and Mae Boontham buffet rice & curry in front of Odeon Market beside the chedi. Expect around 40–50 THB per person, open morning to afternoon.

faq.q: Roughly how much does eating around the chedi cost?
faq.a: If you just graze your way around, about 150–300 THB per person fills you up on a good few things. Noodles and rice & curry run 40–60 THB a plate, fried snacks 80–160 THB a box, and sweets start at just over ten baht.

faq.q: How do shops around the chedi take payment — do they accept transfers?
faq.a: Newer shops and many cafés take QR payments, but most old shops and market stalls are still easier with cash. Carrying cash on you is the smoothest way to go.
